items.title: How to approach an LLD interview
items.summary: A low-level design (LLD) round asks you to turn a vague idea, such as "design a parking lot", into a small set of clean, working classes in about 45 minutes. This chapter gives you a nine-step method you can repeat for any problem, and walks one example (a parking lot) through every step so you can see what each step actually produces.
items.markdown:
A low-level design (LLD) round asks you to turn a vague idea, such as "design a parking lot", into a small set of clean, working classes in about 45 minutes. This chapter gives you a nine-step method you can repeat for any problem, and walks one example (a parking lot) through every step so you can see what each step actually produces.

## What interviewers score

Interviewers are not checking whether you remember pattern names. They are watching how you think. Most rubrics look at five things:

-   **Requirements:** Did you ask good questions and write down what is in and out of scope?
-   **Modelling:** Do your classes match real concepts, and does each class have one clear job?
-   **Extensibility:** Can a new vehicle type or payment method be added by writing a new class instead of editing old ones?
-   **Correctness:** Did you handle edge cases and two users acting at the same time?
-   **Communication:** Did you explain your choices, talk through trade-offs, and take hints well?

Keep these five in mind. Every step below is designed to earn points on at least one of them.

---

## 1. Clarify requirements

**What to do:** Ask questions that change the design, then write down what is in scope and what is out.

**Why:** "Parking lot" can mean a single-level mall lot or a ten-floor airport garage with EV chargers. If you guess, you may design the wrong thing for twenty minutes.

### Example: Parking Lot

Good questions to ask:

-   One floor or many? Different spot sizes?
-   Which vehicles: bikes, cars, trucks?
-   How is the fee calculated: hourly, flat, different per vehicle?
-   Pay at exit only? Cash, card, UPI?
-   Do we need a display board showing free spots?

Then write the answer down where the interviewer can see it:

```text
IN:  multiple floors, 3 spot sizes (SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE),
     bike/car/truck, hourly pricing, pay at exit (cash/card)
OUT: reservations, monthly passes, EV charging
```

**Common mistake:** Asking trivia ("what colour are the tickets?") or asking nothing at all and starting to code.

---

## 2. List use cases

**What to do:** Name the actors (who uses the system) and what each actor can do. Also note one or two non-functional needs, such as "two cars must never get the same spot".

**Why:** Use cases become the public methods of your system. They also give you a checklist to verify your design against later.

### Example: Parking Lot

```text
Driver:    park vehicle, take ticket, pay, exit
Attendant: view free spots, handle lost ticket
Admin:     add floor, add spots, change rates

Non-functional:
- no two vehicles get the same spot (concurrency)
- new vehicle types and pricing rules are easy to add
```

**Common mistake:** Listing twenty use cases. Pick the three or four that matter and say the rest are out of scope.

---

## 3. Find entities and behaviours

**What to do:** Read your requirements and use cases. The **nouns** are candidate classes. The **verbs** are candidate methods.

**Why:** This gives you a starting list quickly, and it keeps your classes named after real things in the problem.

### Example: Parking Lot

```text
Nouns:  ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket,
        Gate, Payment, DisplayBoard, licence plate
Verbs:  park, unpark, assign spot, calculate fee, pay, show free spots
```

Now clean the list:

-   "licence plate" is just a field of `Vehicle`, not a class.
-   "Slot" and "Spot" mean the same thing, so keep one name.
-   "calculate fee" belongs to something that knows about pricing, not to `Vehicle`.

**Common mistake:** Making a class for every noun, or making one giant `ParkingLotManager` that does every verb.

---

## 4. Define relationships

**What to do:** For each pair of related classes, decide: is it **is-a** (inheritance) or **has-a** (composition or association)? How many of each (one, many, optional)?

**Why:** Relationships tell the interviewer who owns what. They also tell you which Java fields and collections to use.

### Example: Parking Lot

```text
ParkingLot  has many   Floor         (lot owns its floors)
Floor       has many   ParkingSpot   (floor owns its spots)
ParkingSpot has 0 or 1 Vehicle       (currently parked car)
Ticket      refers to  1 Vehicle and 1 ParkingSpot
Car, Bike, Truck  is-a  Vehicle
```

**Common mistake:** Using inheritance for reuse, such as `Ticket extends ParkingSpot`. A ticket is not a kind of spot; it *refers to* a spot.

---

## 5. Pick patterns where things vary

**What to do:** Look for places where the requirements say behaviour will differ or grow: "different pricing", "many payment methods", "different ways to pick a spot". Put an interface there. Use a pattern only when it solves one of these stated needs.

**Why:** Interfaces at the right places make the design extensible. Interfaces everywhere make it hard to read.

### Example: Parking Lot

```text
Pricing varies          -> PricingStrategy        (Strategy)
Payment methods vary    -> PaymentProcessor       (Strategy)
Spot choice may vary    -> SpotAssignmentStrategy (Strategy)
Board must update when spots change -> Observer   (optional)
```

Say it out loud in one sentence: "Pricing varies by vehicle type, so I will make it a strategy. Adding a weekend rate is then a new class."

**Common mistake:** Opening with "I'll use Singleton, Factory and Observer" before you know why. Patterns should be the answer to a requirement, not decoration.

---

## 6. Write the core classes and interfaces

**What to do:** Write the key classes with their important fields and methods. Skip getters, setters, and boilerplate unless asked.

**Why:** This is the part the interviewer will read most closely. Small, clear classes with behaviour (not just data) score well.

### Example: Parking Lot

```java
enum SpotSize { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }

abstract class Vehicle {
    private final String plate;
    protected Vehicle(String plate) { this.plate = plate; }
    public String getPlate() { return plate; }
    public abstract SpotSize requiredSize();
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    Car(String plate) { super(plate); }
    public SpotSize requiredSize() { return SpotSize.MEDIUM; }
}

interface PricingStrategy {
    long calculateFee(Ticket ticket, Instant exitTime);
}

interface SpotAssignmentStrategy {
    Optional<ParkingSpot> findSpot(List<Floor> floors, SpotSize size);
}

class ParkingService {
    public Ticket park(Vehicle vehicle) { /* ... */ return null; }
    public Receipt unpark(String ticketId, PaymentProcessor payment) { /* ... */ return null; }
}
```

Notice that `ParkingService` does not contain pricing rules or spot-search rules. It asks its strategies.

**Common mistake:** Writing classes that are only fields plus getters and setters, with all the logic in one service class.

---

## 7. Walk through a use case

**What to do:** Pick the main use case and trace it through your classes, call by call.

**Why:** A walkthrough proves the design works. It also reveals missing methods or a class that is doing too much.

### Example: Parking Lot

```text
Car arrives at entry gate
 -> ParkingService.park(car)
 -> assignmentStrategy.findSpot(floors, MEDIUM)  returns spot F2-17
 -> spot.tryPark(car)                            marks it occupied
 -> new Ticket(car, spot, clock.instant())
 -> displayBoard.update()
 -> ticket returned to driver

Car leaves
 -> ParkingService.unpark(ticketId, cardProcessor)
 -> pricingStrategy.calculateFee(ticket, now)    returns 120
 -> cardProcessor.pay(120)
 -> spot.release()
```

**Common mistake:** Skipping the walkthrough. Many designs look fine as boxes and fall apart when you trace a real request.

---

## 8. Concurrency and edge cases

**What to do:** Ask "what if two people do this at the same time?" and "what if something goes wrong halfway?" Find the shared state and protect it.

**Why:** This is where strong candidates separate from average ones. Booking-style problems almost always have a race condition.

### The problem

Two entry gates call `findSpot` at the same moment. Both see spot F2-17 as free. Both send a car there.

### Better design

Make "check and occupy" a single atomic step:

```java
class ParkingSpot {
    private final String id;
    private final SpotSize size;
    private Vehicle vehicle;

    ParkingSpot(String id, SpotSize size) {
        this.id = id;
        this.size = size;
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryPark(Vehicle v) {
        if (vehicle != null) {
            return false;   // someone else got it first
        }
        vehicle = v;
        return true;
    }

    public synchronized void release() {
        vehicle = null;
    }
}
```

If `tryPark` returns false, the service simply tries the next free spot. Then list edge cases briefly: lot is full, lost ticket, paying twice, payment fails after the car has left.

**Common mistake:** Never mentioning concurrency, or saying "I'll make everything synchronized" without naming what is shared.

---

## 9. Discuss extensions

**What to do:** Show how the design handles a new requirement with minimal change. Then summarise your design in two or three sentences.

**Why:** "How would you add X?" is almost always the last question. A good answer points to an existing extension point.

### Example: Parking Lot

-   **Weekend pricing:** add `WeekendPricing implements PricingStrategy`. Nothing else changes.
-   **UPI payment:** add `UpiProcessor implements PaymentProcessor`.
-   **EV charging:** add an `EV` spot type and let the assignment strategy filter for it.
-   **Many servers instead of one:** the `synchronized` lock becomes a database row lock or a distributed lock.

**Common mistake:** Answering "I'd add an else-if in the fee method". That tells the interviewer the design is not open for extension.

---

## A simple time plan

```text
 0-5   min  Clarify requirements, write IN/OUT
 5-10  min  Use cases, entities, relationships
10-15  min  Variation points and interfaces
15-35  min  Core classes, walkthrough
35-45  min  Concurrency, edge cases, extensions, summary
```

You do not need to follow it exactly. The point is to leave time for concurrency and extensions, which is where many candidates run out of time.

---

## In an LLD interview

-   **Parking Lot, Elevator, Vending Machine:** state matters (spot free or occupied, elevator moving or idle, machine waiting for coins or dispensing). Walk through the state changes in step 7.
-   **BookMyShow, Splitwise:** the concurrency step is central. Two users booking the last seat, or two people editing the same expense, is the question the interviewer is waiting for.
-   **Notification System, Rate Limiter:** the variation points are obvious (channels, algorithms). Show one interface and two implementations early.
-   **Chess:** entities and relationships take most of the time. Keep move rules in the pieces, not in one huge `Game` class.
-   In every problem, state each design decision with its reason in one sentence.

## At a glance

| Step | Core idea | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Clarify | Agree on scope | What is in and what is out? |
| 2. Use cases | Who does what | What are the 3-4 main flows? |
| 3. Entities | Nouns become classes, verbs become methods | Is this a class or just a field? |
| 4. Relationships | Is-a vs. has-a, and how many | Who owns whom? |
| 5. Patterns | Interfaces where behaviour varies | Did a requirement ask for this? |
| 6. Core classes | Small classes with behaviour | Is any class doing too much? |
| 7. Walkthrough | Trace one request | Does every call have a home? |
| 8. Concurrency | Protect shared state | What if two users do this at once? |
| 9. Extensions | Add, don't edit | What changes for a new variant? |

## Final memory aid

-   **Ask** before you design.
-   **Nouns** become classes, **verbs** become methods.
-   **Interfaces** only where things vary.
-   **Walk** one request through the code.
-   **Race:** find it and fix it.
-   **Extend** by adding a class, not an else-if.

items.title: OOP in Java: pillars, composition and interfaces
items.summary: Object-oriented programming is the toolkit you use in every LLD answer. Most candidates can name the four pillars; this chapter shows when to use each one, what goes wrong when you misuse it, and how composition, interfaces, equals/hashCode and immutability fit in.

items.title: Class relationships and UML diagrams
items.summary: A class diagram is the quickest way to show an interviewer how your classes connect: who owns whom, who just uses whom, and where the extension points are. This chapter explains the seven relationships you need, with a plain-English test, Java code and the matching UML symbol for each, then shows how to draw a clean diagram in an interview.
items.markdown:
A class diagram is the quickest way to show an interviewer how your classes connect: who owns whom, who just uses whom, and where the extension points are. This chapter explains the seven relationships you need, with a plain-English test, Java code and the matching UML symbol for each, then shows how to draw a clean diagram in an interview.

## Reading a class box

Every class in a UML diagram is a box with three parts: the name, the fields, and the methods.

```text
+-----------------------------+
| Ticket                      |   <- class name
+-----------------------------+
| - id: String                |   <- fields: visibility name: type
| - entryTime: Instant        |
+-----------------------------+
| + close(exitTime): Receipt  |   <- methods
+-----------------------------+
```

Visibility markers: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected. Interfaces are marked `<<interface>>` above the name. In an interview, show only the fields and methods that explain the design. Nobody wants every getter.

---

## 1. Association

**Definition:** One class holds a reference to another, and both can exist on their own.

**Ask:** "Does A keep a reference to B, and does B live its own life without A?" If yes, it is an association.

### Example in Java

```java
class Car {
    private final String plate;
    Car(String plate) { this.plate = plate; }
}

class Driver {
    private final String name;
    private Car assignedCar;   // Driver knows its Car

    Driver(String name) { this.name = name; }

    public void assign(Car car) {
        this.assignedCar = car;
    }
}
```

The driver knows about the car, but neither owns the other. Removing the driver does not remove the car.

### UML notation

```text
+--------+ 1         0..1 +-----+
| Driver |--------------->| Car |
+--------+                +-----+
solid line; the arrow shows Driver can reach Car
```

**Key takeaway:** Association is a lasting "knows about" link between two independent objects. Prefer one-way links; add the reverse direction only if a use case needs it.

---

## 2. Aggregation

**Definition:** A whole–part association where the parts can exist without the whole, and may even belong to several wholes.

**Ask:** "Is this has-a, and can the part live alone?" If yes, it is aggregation.

### Example in Java

```java
class Player {
    private final String name;
    Player(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

class Team {
    private final List<Player> players = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addPlayer(Player player) {   // created outside, passed in
        players.add(player);
    }
}
```

If the team is disbanded, the players still exist and can join another team.

### UML notation

```text
+------+ 1         0..* +--------+
| Team |<>--------------| Player |
+------+                +--------+
hollow (empty) diamond on the whole's side
```

**Key takeaway:** Aggregation is a loose has-a. The part is created elsewhere and passed in.

---

## 3. Composition

**Definition:** A strong whole–part relationship where the whole creates and owns its parts, and the parts die with the whole.

**Ask:** "Is this has-a, and does the part make no sense without the whole?" If yes, it is composition.

### Example in Java

```java
class OrderLine {
    private final String product;
    private final int quantity;

    OrderLine(String product, int quantity) {
        this.product = product;
        this.quantity = quantity;
    }
}

class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addLine(String product, int quantity) {
        lines.add(new OrderLine(product, quantity));   // created inside
    }

    public List<OrderLine> getLines() {
        return List.copyOf(lines);                     // never shared for editing
    }
}
```

An order line belongs to exactly one order. Delete the order and its lines go with it.

### UML notation

```text
+-------+ 1         1..* +-----------+
| Order |<#>-------------| OrderLine |
+-------+                +-----------+
filled (solid black) diamond on the whole's side
```

**Key takeaway:** Composition means ownership. The whole creates the part inside itself and never hands it out to be shared.

### Aggregation vs. Composition

-   **Aggregation asks:** Can the part survive and be shared if the whole goes away? (`Team` and `Player`, `Library` and `Book`)
-   **Composition asks:** Is the part created, owned and destroyed by exactly one whole? (`Order` and `OrderLine`, `Board` and `Cell`)

A quick code check: if the part is passed into the constructor or an `add` method, it is usually aggregation. If the whole calls `new` for the part itself, it is usually composition.

---

## 4. Dependency

**Definition:** A class uses another only temporarily, as a method parameter, local variable or return type, without keeping a reference.

**Ask:** "Does A only touch B inside a method call?" If yes, it is a dependency.

### Example in Java

```java
class Receipt {
    private final double amount;
    Receipt(double amount) { this.amount = amount; }
    public double getAmount() { return amount; }
}

class ReceiptPrinter {
    public void print(Receipt receipt) {   // used only during the call
        System.out.println("Paid: " + receipt.getAmount());
    }
}
```

`ReceiptPrinter` has no `Receipt` field. If `Receipt` changes, the printer might need to change, but there is no lasting link.

### UML notation

```text
+----------------+          +---------+
| ReceiptPrinter |- - - - ->| Receipt |
+----------------+          +---------+
dashed line with an open arrow
```

**Key takeaway:** Dependency is the weakest relationship: "uses for a moment". It is the safest kind of coupling to have.

### Association vs. Dependency

-   **Association asks:** Does A store B in a field, so the link lasts beyond one call?
-   **Dependency asks:** Does A only receive or create B inside a method and then let it go?

In Java the test is simple: a field means association; only a parameter or local variable means dependency.

---

## 5. Inheritance (generalization)

**Definition:** A subclass is a more specific kind of its parent class. In Java this is `extends`.

**Ask:** "Is A truly a kind of B, and can A keep every promise B makes?" If yes, it is inheritance.

### Example in Java

```java
abstract class Vehicle {
    private final String plate;

    protected Vehicle(String plate) { this.plate = plate; }

    public abstract SpotSize requiredSize();
}

class Truck extends Vehicle {
    Truck(String plate) { super(plate); }

    public SpotSize requiredSize() { return SpotSize.LARGE; }
}
```

### UML notation

```text
   +---------+
   | Vehicle |   {abstract}
   +---------+
        ^
        |        solid line, hollow triangle
        |        points to the parent
   +---------+
   |  Truck  |
   +---------+
```

**Key takeaway:** Inheritance is the strongest coupling there is. Draw it only for a real is-a relationship, not to reuse a few methods.

---

## 6. Realization (implements)

**Definition:** A class promises to fulfil the contract of an interface. In Java this is `implements`.

**Ask:** "Does A provide the behaviour that interface B describes?" If yes, it is realization.

### Example in Java

```java
interface PaymentProcessor {
    void pay(double amount);
}

class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
    public void pay(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Charging card: " + amount);
    }
}

class UpiProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
    public void pay(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Collecting via UPI: " + amount);
    }
}
```

### UML notation

```text
      +----------------------+
      |    <<interface>>     |
      |   PaymentProcessor   |
      +----------------------+
           ^            ^
           :            :      dashed line, hollow triangle
  +---------------+ +--------------+
  | CardProcessor | | UpiProcessor |
  +---------------+ +--------------+
```

**Key takeaway:** Realization is how you draw extension points. The interface with several implementations underneath is the picture of the open/closed principle.

---

## 7. Multiplicity

**Definition:** Multiplicity says how many objects can be on each end of a relationship.

**Ask:** "For one A, how many B can there be: exactly one, zero or one, or many?"

Common values:

-   `1` exactly one
-   `0..1` optional, at most one
-   `*` or `0..*` zero or more
-   `1..*` at least one
-   `0..5` a range (a business rule, such as "at most 5 books on loan")

### Example in Java

```java
class ParkingSpot {
    private Vehicle vehicle;              // 0..1: may be empty
}

class Floor {
    private final int number;             // 1: always set
    private final List<ParkingSpot> spots; // 1..*: at least one spot

    Floor(int number, List<ParkingSpot> spots) {
        if (spots.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Floor needs spots");
        this.number = number;
        this.spots = List.copyOf(spots);
    }
}
```

### UML notation

```text
+------------+ 1       1..* +-------+ 1       1..* +-------------+
| ParkingLot |<#>-----------| Floor |<#>-----------| ParkingSpot |
+------------+              +-------+              +-------------+
```

**Key takeaway:** Multiplicity drives your Java types: `1` is a required `final` field, `0..1` is a nullable field (or `Optional` from a getter), and `*` is a `List`, `Set` or `Map` chosen by how you look things up.

---

## Drawing a class diagram in an interview

You have a few minutes and a whiteboard or text box. Aim for clarity, not completeness.

**Include:**

-   The 6–12 classes that carry the design (for a parking lot: `ParkingLot`, `Floor`, `ParkingSpot`, `Vehicle`, `Ticket`, `ParkingService`, and the strategy interfaces).
-   Interfaces at variation points, with two implementations shown under each.
-   Composition vs. aggregation where ownership matters.
-   Multiplicity on the important links.
-   Only the key fields and methods.

**Skip:**

-   Getters, setters, constructors and `toString`.
-   Every exception class and helper.
-   Arrows in both directions unless a use case needs them.
-   Perfect notation. A clear label like "owns" or "uses" is better than a wrong symbol.

A good order is: draw the main entities first, then connect them, then add the interfaces, then write multiplicities. Talk while you draw.

---

## In an LLD interview

-   **Parking Lot, Elevator:** composition from building to floor to spot (or to elevator car); association from ticket to vehicle; inheritance for vehicle types.
-   **BookMyShow:** `Show` aggregates `Screen` (screens outlive shows); a `Booking` is associated with seats and a user; payment is a realized interface.
-   **Splitwise:** `Group` aggregates `User` (users exist outside a group); an `Expense` composes its `Split` lines.
-   **Chess, Vending Machine:** `Board` composes `Cell`s; `Piece` uses inheritance; the machine's states can be drawn as realizations of a `State` interface.
-   **Notification System, Rate Limiter:** the key picture is one interface (`Channel`, `RateLimiter`) with several implementations underneath.

## At a glance

| Relationship | Core idea | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Association | Holds a reference, both independent | Is B stored in a field, and does B live alone? |
| Aggregation | Has-a, part can live alone | If the whole goes, does the part survive? |
| Composition | Has-a, part dies with whole | Does the whole create and own the part? |
| Dependency | Uses briefly | Is B only a parameter or local variable? |
| Inheritance | Is-a (`extends`) | Can the child keep every promise of the parent? |
| Realization | Implements a contract | Is this an interface with several implementations? |
| Multiplicity | How many on each end | One, optional, or many? |

## Final memory aid

-   **Association:** knows
-   **Aggregation:** has, can leave (hollow diamond)
-   **Composition:** owns, dies together (filled diamond)
-   **Dependency:** uses for a moment (dashed arrow)
-   **Inheritance:** is-a (solid line, hollow triangle)
-   **Realization:** implements (dashed line, hollow triangle)
-   **Multiplicity:** how many, which drives the Java type

items.title: SOLID principles with Java examples
items.summary: SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help make software easier to maintain, extend, test, and understand. This chapter explains each principle with a violation, a better design and a key takeaway, then shows how to use SOLID to justify your decisions in an LLD interview.

items.title: Creational patterns: Factory, Builder, Singleton and friends
items.summary: Creational patterns are about how objects get created: which concrete class is chosen, how a complicated object is put together, and how many instances exist. The common goal is to keep the code that uses an object from caring about the code that builds it. When creation lives in one place, adding a new variant means changing one file instead of hunting down every new.

items.title: Structural patterns: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Composite, Proxy, Bridge
items.summary: Structural patterns are about how classes and objects are combined into bigger structures without becoming rigid. They cover wrapping an object to add behaviour, translating one interface into another, hiding a complicated subsystem behind a simple entry point, and treating a group of things like a single thing. Most clean integrations in an LLD answer use at least one of them.

items.title: Behavioral patterns I: Strategy, State, Observer, Command
items.summary: Behavioral patterns are about how objects share work and talk to each other. Strategy, State, Observer and Command show up in almost every LLD interview problem, from parking lot pricing to elevator control to undo in a game. If you can spot them from the wording of the requirements, half the design is already done.

items.title: Behavioral patterns II: Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor
items.summary: These six patterns come up less often than Strategy or State, but when a problem has the right shape they give the cleanest answer. They cover passing a request through a series of handlers, fixing the steps of an algorithm, walking a custom collection, coordinating many objects, saving snapshots, and adding operations to a set of types. Each one below starts with the messy version so you can see exactly what the pattern fixes.

items.title: Concurrency for LLD: races, locks, atomics and holds
items.summary: Almost every LLD problem has one moment where two users reach for the same thing at the same time: the last seat, the last parking spot, the same wallet balance. This chapter shows how to spot that moment, which Java tool fixes it most simply, and how to explain the choice in plain words. Each idea comes with a small "what goes wrong" example and a better version.

items.title: Modelling details interviewers notice: money, time, IDs, enums, errors
items.summary: Interviewers often judge an LLD answer by small details: how you store money, which time type you pick, what an ID looks like, and what happens when something goes wrong. Each of these takes only seconds to get right, and each one signals that you have shipped real systems. This chapter walks through them with small examples of the problem and a better design.

items.title: How to approach a system design interview
items.summary: A system design interview is deliberately open-ended: "Design a URL shortener" could fill a week. The interviewer wants to see how you turn that vagueness into a clear plan, back your choices with numbers, and go deep where it matters. This chapter gives you an eight-step method, shown on one running example (a URL shortener like bit.ly), plus what interviewers score and a time plan.
items.markdown:
A system design interview is deliberately open-ended: "Design a URL shortener" could fill a week. The interviewer wants to see how you turn that vagueness into a clear plan, back your choices with numbers, and go deep where it matters. This chapter gives you an eight-step method, shown on one running example (a URL shortener like bit.ly), plus what interviewers score and a time plan.

## 1. Requirements

**Definition:** Agree on what the system must do (functional) and how well it must do it (non-functional) before drawing anything.

Functional requirements are the 3-5 core use cases. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) are the qualities that drive the architecture: scale, latency, availability, consistency and durability. Think of an architect asking "how many people will live here?" before choosing between a cottage and a tower.

### The problem

```text
Interviewer: Design a URL shortener.
Candidate:   OK, we'll have Kafka, Cassandra, Kubernetes, and microservices for
             users, links, analytics, billing...
```

Twenty minutes later the interviewer asks "how many links per day?" and the candidate does not know. Nothing on the board can be justified, because nothing was asked.

### Better design

```text
Functional:   create short link (optional custom alias, optional expiry)
              redirect short -> long
              basic click count per link
Out of scope: user accounts, dashboards, billing   (say this out loud)
NFRs:         100M new links/month, reads ~100x writes
              redirect p99 < 50 ms, highly available (redirects matter more than creates)
              a created link must never be lost; slightly stale analytics are fine
```

Every later decision can now point back to a line on this list. Parking features explicitly keeps the scope small and shows judgement.

**Key takeaway:** Spend about 5 minutes on requirements, and write down what is out of scope.

---

## 2. Estimation

**Definition:** Quick arithmetic that turns requirements into numbers: requests per second (QPS), storage, bandwidth and cache size.

The goal is the right order of magnitude, not precision. An estimate is only useful if it changes a decision, so stop once it has.

### The problem

A candidate spends eight minutes computing storage to three decimal places, then draws the same system they would have drawn anyway. The numbers never influence anything.

### Better design

```text
Writes: 100M / month / 2.5M s ~ 40/s        (peak ~100/s)  -> one DB primary is fine
Reads:  40 x 100 ~ 4,000/s                  (peak ~10-20k) -> add a cache
Data:   100M x 12 x 5 yrs = 6B links x 500 B = 3 TB         -> plan to shard by code later
Codes:  62^7 ~ 3.5 trillion >> 6 billion                    -> 7 base62 chars suffice
```

Each line ends with a decision. That arrow is what the interviewer is listening for. The next article covers estimation in depth.

**Key takeaway:** Every number should end with "so we will...".

---

## 3. API design

**Definition:** Define the contract between clients and the system before designing the internals.

The API fixes the inputs, outputs and error cases. It also surfaces hidden requirements such as idempotency (sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once) and rate limits.

### The problem

The candidate says "there's a create endpoint and a get endpoint" and moves on. Later nobody knows whether redirects return 301 or 302, or what happens when a custom alias is already taken.

### Better design

```http
POST /v1/urls
  Idempotency-Key: 7f3c...
  { "longUrl": "...", "customAlias": "sale24", "expiresAt": "2026-12-31T00:00:00Z" }
  -> 201 { "code": "sale24", "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/sale24" }
  -> 409 Conflict if the alias is taken

GET /{code}
  -> 302 Location: <longUrl>     (302 so every click reaches us and is counted)
  -> 404 if unknown, 410 Gone if expired
```

The 301 vs 302 choice is a real trade-off: browsers cache a 301 (permanent redirect), which saves load on you but hides later clicks from your analytics.

**Key takeaway:** Write 2-4 endpoints with status codes, plus one sentence on auth, idempotency and rate limits.

---

## 4. Data model

**Definition:** List the entities and their access patterns, then choose storage that fits those patterns.

An access pattern answers "how will we read and write this data?", for example "fetch by code, 10k times a second". Access patterns choose the database, not brand names.

### The problem

"We'll use Cassandra because it scales." When asked how a custom alias is checked for uniqueness, the candidate has no answer, because the choice came before the questions.

### Better design

```sql
-- point lookup by code at ~10k QPS, insert at ~40/s
CREATE TABLE url (
  code        VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,   -- also enforces alias uniqueness
  long_url    TEXT        NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
  expires_at  TIMESTAMP   NULL
);
-- clicks: append-only, aggregated later -> queue + analytics store, not this table
```

The `url` data is a pure key-value lookup, so a relational database or a key-value store both work. Click events have a completely different pattern (huge volume of appends, read only in aggregate), so they get different storage.

**Key takeaway:** Say the access pattern first, then the store.

---

## 5. High-level design

**Definition:** Draw the main components and walk one write and one read through them.

Start with the simplest design that meets the numbers. Every box must earn its place.

### The problem

A diagram with 15 boxes and no arrows explained. The interviewer cannot tell what happens when a user clicks a link.

### Better design

```text
Client -> DNS -> Load balancer -> App servers (stateless)
                                    |-- read  -> Redis cache -> (miss) DB replica
                                    |-- write -> DB primary
                                    |-- click event -> Queue -> Workers -> Analytics DB

Read:  GET /abc123 -> cache hit (most requests) -> 302; miss -> replica -> fill cache
Write: POST -> generate code -> insert into primary -> 201
```

Walking a read and a write proves the diagram works and gives the interviewer natural places to ask "what if?".

**Key takeaway:** Simple first, then narrate one request end to end.

---

## 6. Deep dives

**Definition:** Spend the biggest block of time on the 2-3 hardest parts of this particular problem.

For each part use the same shape: options, trade-offs, choice, failure handling. Offer the interviewer a choice of topic if they seem to have one in mind.

### The problem

"We'll generate a random code." How are collisions handled? What if two servers produce the same code? The hard part is waved away.

### Better design

```text
Unique code generation:
  a) hash(longUrl), take 7 chars  -> collisions; must check and retry
  b) random 7 chars               -> collisions rare but possible; check on insert
  c) counter + base62 encoding    -> no collisions; the counter is a hotspot / SPOF
Choice: (c) with ID ranges - each app server leases 1,000 IDs at a time from a
        central counter. A crashed server wastes at most 1,000 IDs, which is fine.
Note:   sequential codes are guessable; shuffle the bits if that matters.
```

Other typical deep dives here: hot links and the caching strategy, and the analytics pipeline.

**Key takeaway:** Options, trade-offs, choice, failure handling, every time.

---

## 7. Bottlenecks and failures

**Definition:** Ask "what breaks first, and what happens when each box dies?"

A single point of failure (SPOF) is a component whose failure takes the whole system down. Every box you drew is a candidate.

### The problem

The design has one Redis node and one DB primary. The interviewer says "Redis just died", and the candidate realises all 20k reads/s now hit the database at once.

### Better design

```text
Cache down      -> Redis replica + failover; DB replicas sized to survive a cold cache
DB primary down -> automatic failover to a replica; creates fail briefly, redirects continue
Queue down      -> click events buffered or dropped; redirects unaffected
Hot link        -> served from cache (and from a CDN if 301 is acceptable)
Monitor         -> p99 redirect latency, error rate, cache hit ratio, queue lag
```

Separating the critical path (redirects) from non-critical work (analytics) lets parts fail without a full outage.

**Key takeaway:** Name each SPOF and say what degrades, not just what breaks.

---

## 8. Trade-offs and wrap-up

**Definition:** Summarise the key decisions, what each one cost, and how the design would evolve.

This is where senior candidates stand out. A choice without a stated cost sounds like a guess.

### The problem

"So that's the design." The interviewer has to drag the reasoning out with questions.

### Better design

```text
302 not 301      : + accurate analytics       - more load on our servers
Counter + base62 : + no collisions            - guessable codes, needs a counter service
Cache-aside      : + fast reads               - an edited link may be stale for the TTL
Next steps       : multi-region read replicas, CDN at the edge, abuse/spam detection
```

**Key takeaway:** For every major choice, say what you gained and what you paid.

---

## 9. What interviewers score

**Definition:** Interviewers grade signals, not a "correct" diagram; there usually is none.

### The signals

- **Problem navigation:** clarifying scope, stating assumptions, staying aligned with requirements.
- **Breadth:** knowing the standard building blocks (cache, queue, replicas, CDN) and when each fits.
- **Depth:** explaining real mechanisms on 2-3 hard parts instead of buzzwords.
- **Trade-offs:** naming alternatives and why one wins, ideally with numbers.
- **Operational maturity:** failures, monitoring, deployments, data growth.
- **Communication:** driving the discussion, thinking aloud, checking in, following hints.

A question like "what if a celebrity shares a link?" is a hint about hot keys, not an attack on your design. Follow it.

**Key takeaway:** At senior level, driving the conversation and justifying trade-offs matter more than the boxes.

---

## 10. A time plan

**Definition:** A rough minute budget so you never run out of time before the deep dive.

| Step | 45 min | 60 min |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | 5 | 6 |
| Estimation | 3 | 4 |
| API + data model | 6 | 8 |
| High-level design | 8 | 10 |
| Deep dives | 15 | 22 |
| Bottlenecks + trade-offs | 5 | 7 |
| Buffer for questions | 3 | 3 |

Check in at each transition: "I'll move to the data model unless you'd like more on the API?"

**Key takeaway:** Protect the deep-dive time; it carries the most weight.

---

## In an HLD interview

- **URL Shortener:** the full method above; the deep dive is code generation and the 301 vs 302 choice.
- **News Feed / Chat:** requirements decide everything (fan-out on write vs read, delivery and ordering guarantees), so spend the full 5 minutes there.
- **Payment System / Seat Reservation:** the NFRs are about correctness, so the deep dive is idempotency and preventing double charging or double booking.
- **YouTube / Netflix:** estimation shows bandwidth dominates, which justifies a CDN before anything else.
- **What to SAY:** "Let me confirm the requirements and rough scale first, then I'll sketch a simple design and we can go deep on the hardest parts."

## At a glance

| Concept | Core idea | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | Scope and NFRs first | What is in, what is out, how big, how strict? |
| Estimation | Numbers that decide | Which decision does this number change? |
| API | Contract before internals | What are the inputs, outputs and errors? |
| Data model | Access patterns pick storage | How is this data read and written? |
| High-level design | Simple, then walk a request | Can I narrate one read and one write? |
| Deep dives | 2-3 hardest parts | Options, trade-offs, choice, failure? |
| Bottlenecks | SPOFs and degradation | What happens when this box dies? |
| Trade-offs | Every choice has a cost | What did I gain and what did I pay? |

## Final memory aid

- **Ask** before you draw
- **Count** only what changes a decision
- **Contract** before internals
- **Access patterns** pick the database
- **Simple first**, then walk a request through it
- **Go deep** on the hard part: options, trade-offs, choice, failure
- **Break it:** every box can die
- **Say the cost** of every choice

items.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
items.summary: Back-of-the-envelope estimation turns vague scale ("millions of users") into numbers that justify the architecture: how many servers, whether data fits in memory, whether one database survives the write rate. Interviewers want the right order of magnitude, reached quickly and out loud, not precision. This chapter covers the numbers to memorise, the formulas, worked examples and the common mistakes.
items.markdown:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation turns vague scale ("millions of users") into numbers that justify the architecture: how many servers, whether data fits in memory, whether one database survives the write rate. Interviewers want the right order of magnitude, reached quickly and out loud, not precision. This chapter covers the numbers to memorise, the formulas, worked examples and the common mistakes.

## 1. Powers of two and ten

**Definition:** Each size unit is about 1,000 times the previous one, so you can work in powers of ten and stop counting zeros.

Strictly, 1 KB is 2^10 = 1,024 bytes, but in estimation 1,000 is close enough. Scientific notation (4 x 10^9 instead of 4,000,000,000) is the best defence against arithmetic slips.

### The problem

```text
6,000,000,000 links x 500 bytes = 3,000,000,000,000 bytes = ... 300 GB? 3 TB? 30 TB?
```

Counting zeros on a whiteboard under pressure goes wrong easily, and a 10x error changes the design.

### Better design

```text
Power  Approx  Unit  Name
2^10   10^3    KB    thousand
2^20   10^6    MB    million
2^30   10^9    GB    billion
2^40   10^12   TB    trillion
2^50   10^15   PB    quadrillion

6 x 10^9 x 5 x 10^2 B = 30 x 10^11 B = 3 x 10^12 B = 3 TB
```

Multiply the leading digits, add the exponents, then map the exponent back to a unit.

**Key takeaway:** Write exponents, not zeros.

---

## 2. Latency numbers

**Definition:** Rough costs of common operations, which differ from each other by orders of magnitude.

These numbers explain why we cache, why we keep data close to users and why we batch. Exact values depend on hardware; the ratios are what matter.

```text
L1 cache reference                   ~1 ns
Main memory reference                ~100 ns
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory   ~10 us    (us = microsecond)
SSD random read                      ~20-100 us
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD      ~50 us - 1 ms
Round trip in the same datacenter    ~0.5 ms
HDD disk seek                        ~5-10 ms
Round trip India <-> US              ~150-250 ms
```

### The problem

A page makes 10 sequential calls from Mumbai to a database in Virginia. At ~200 ms per round trip, the page spends 2 seconds just waiting on the network.

### Better design

Put a cache or read replica in the user's region (~0.5-1 ms per call), or batch the 10 calls into one. The same work now costs a few milliseconds of network time.

**Key takeaway:** Memory is fast, disk is slower, crossing an ocean is very slow; design to avoid the slow trips.

---

## 3. QPS from daily active users

**Definition:** Average QPS = (daily active users x actions per user per day) / seconds in a day.

A day has 86,400 seconds; round it to 10^5 and say so. Handy shortcuts: 1 million requests/day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion/day is about 12,000 per second.

### The problem

"We have 10 million users, so 10 million QPS." Not every user is active today, and an active user does not make a request every second.

### Better design

```text
DAU = 10M, each user makes 20 requests/day
Daily requests = 10^7 x 20 = 2 x 10^8
Average QPS    = 2 x 10^8 / 10^5 = 2,000 QPS
```

Then split reads from writes, because they often differ by 10-1000x and scale differently.

**Key takeaway:** Daily events divided by 10^5 gives average QPS.

---

## 4. Peak factor

**Definition:** Peak traffic is the average multiplied by a factor: typically 2-3x for normal daily cycles, 10x or more for flash events.

Traffic follows the day: quiet at 4 a.m., busy at 9 p.m. Events such as a cricket final, a flash sale or a concert ticket release spike far beyond that.

### The problem

The system is sized for the 2,000 QPS average. Every evening it sees 6,000 QPS and starts timing out.

### Better design

```text
Average 2,000 QPS x peak factor 3 = 6,000 QPS   (daily peak)
Flash sale x10                    = 20,000 QPS  (absorb with a queue or autoscaling)
Size for the peak, then add 1.5-2x headroom for failures and deploys.
```

**Trade-offs:**
- Permanently sizing for rare spikes wastes money; queues and autoscaling absorb them more cheaply.

**Key takeaway:** Design for peak, not average.

---

## 5. Storage and bandwidth

**Definition:** Storage = new objects per day x size x retention x replication. Bandwidth = requests per second x payload size.

Replication (usually 3 copies) and index or row overhead (often up to 2x) are easy to forget and together can multiply the total by about 6.

### The problem

```text
"Egress is 1 GB/s, so a 1 Gbps link is enough."
```

GB is gigabytes, Gbps is gigabits. 1 GB/s is 8 Gbps. Mixing bits and bytes is an 8x error.

### Better design

```text
Photo app: 10M uploads/day x 500 KB = 5 x 10^12 B = 5 TB/day raw
Per year:  5 TB x 365 ~ 1.8 PB; x3 replicas ~ 5.5 PB     -> object storage, tiering
Ingress:   10^7 / 10^5 s = 100 uploads/s x 500 KB = 50 MB/s = 400 Mbps
Egress:    each photo viewed 20x -> 2,000 views/s x 500 KB = 1 GB/s = 8 Gbps -> CDN
```

**Key takeaway:** Count replicas and overhead, and multiply bytes by 8 to get bits.

---

## 6. Cache sizing

**Definition:** Cache size is roughly the hot fraction of daily reads (often 20%) times the object size.

The 80/20 rule says a small share of items gets most of the traffic. Caching that share gives most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

### The problem

"Let's cache everything." For the URL shortener that means 3 TB of RAM, mostly holding links nobody clicks.

### Better design

```text
Reads/day = 4,000 QPS x 10^5 s = 4 x 10^8
Hot 20%   = 8 x 10^7 links x 500 B = 4 x 10^10 B = 40 GB
-> fits on one or two cache nodes (64 GB RAM each), plus replicas
```

This is an upper bound that assumes every read is a different link; repeated clicks make the real hot set smaller still.

**Key takeaway:** Cache the hot set, not the whole dataset.

---

## 7. Worked examples

**Definition:** Server count = peak QPS / capacity per server x headroom.

Capacity per node depends heavily on the work per request, so always state it as an assumption.

### Server count

```text
Peak 20,000 QPS; assume one app server handles ~2,000 QPS
20,000 / 2,000 = 10 servers; x2 headroom = ~20 servers, autoscaled
```

### Chat app (WhatsApp-like)

```text
500M DAU x 40 messages/day = 2 x 10^10 messages/day
QPS:     2 x 10^10 / 10^5 = 200,000/s average, ~500k at peak -> heavy sharding
Storage: 2 x 10^10 x 200 B = 4 TB/day ~ 1.5 PB/year before replication
Online:  30% of DAU at peak = 150M sockets; ~500k per gateway -> ~300 gateway servers
```

### Single-node ballparks (state them as assumptions)

| Component | Rough capacity |
|---|---|
| Stateless API server | 1k-10k simple requests/s |
| MySQL / PostgreSQL | ~5k-20k simple writes/s; many more cached reads |
| Redis | ~100k+ ops/s per node |
| One server's RAM | 64-256 GB typical |
| 1 Gbps network link | ~125 MB/s |

**Key takeaway:** Peak divided by per-node capacity, times headroom, gives the node count.

---

## 8. Rounding rules and common mistakes

**Definition:** Round aggressively and openly, keep one significant digit, and stop when a decision is made.

### Rounding rules

- 86,400 s/day -> 10^5; 2.6M s/month -> 2.5 x 10^6; 31.5M s/year -> 3 x 10^7.
- Round sizes to friendly numbers (480 bytes -> 500 B).
- Round in the safe direction for the decision (overestimate load when sizing).
- Say each rounding out loud so the interviewer can follow and correct you.

### Common mistakes

- Designing for the average instead of the peak.
- Forgetting replication and index overhead.
- Mixing bits and bytes.
- Not separating reads from writes.
- Spending minutes on arithmetic that changes no decision.

**Key takeaway:** One significant digit, assumptions on the board, then move on.

---

## In an HLD interview

- **URL Shortener:** 40 writes/s and 4k reads/s show one DB plus a cache is enough; 6B records justify 7-character codes.
- **YouTube / Netflix:** egress measured in terabits per second proves a CDN is mandatory, not optional.
- **Chat / WhatsApp:** 150M concurrent connections justify a separate connection-gateway tier.
- **Rate Limiter / Distributed Cache:** estimate keys x bytes per key to show the counters fit in memory.
- **What to SAY:** "About 10^5 seconds a day, so 2 x 10^8 requests is roughly 2k QPS average and 6k at peak; one DB primary handles that, so I won't shard on day one."

## At a glance

| Concept | Core idea | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Powers of ten | 10^3 per unit step | Am I adding exponents, not counting zeros? |
| Latency numbers | Memory << disk << network | Which slow trip can I avoid? |
| QPS | Daily events / 10^5 | Have I split reads from writes? |
| Peak factor | 2-3x daily, 10x+ events | Am I sizing for the peak? |
| Storage | Count x size x retention x replicas | Did I include replication and overhead? |
| Bandwidth | QPS x payload | Bits or bytes? |
| Cache sizing | Hot 20% of reads | Does the hot set fit in RAM? |
| Server count | Peak / capacity x headroom | What per-node capacity am I assuming? |

## Final memory aid

- **Day:** 10^5 seconds
- **1M/day:** about 12 per second
- **Peak:** 2-3x, flash events 10x
- **Storage:** count x size x retention x 3
- **Bandwidth:** bytes x 8 = bits
- **Cache:** the hot 20%
- **Servers:** peak / capacity x 2
- **Stop** when the number has made a decision

items.title: Scalability, availability, reliability and latency
items.summary: Every architecture decision trades among four qualities: scalability (handling growth), availability (being up), reliability (being correct over time) and latency (being fast). This chapter explains each one in plain terms, shows a small failure and its fix, and gives you the numbers interviewers expect. Most HLD answers are built from these ideas.
items.markdown:
Every architecture decision trades among four qualities: scalability (handling growth), availability (being up), reliability (being correct over time) and latency (being fast). This chapter explains each one in plain terms, shows a small failure and its fix, and gives you the numbers interviewers expect. Most HLD answers are built from these ideas.

## 1. Vertical vs. horizontal scaling

**Definition:** Vertical scaling means a bigger machine; horizontal scaling means more machines sharing the load.

Vertical scaling (scale up) is like replacing a small shop counter with a bigger one: simple, but there is a limit to how big one counter can get. Horizontal scaling (scale out) is opening more counters: almost no ceiling, but you need someone at the door directing customers.

### The problem

```text
One server, 16 cores, handles 3,000 QPS. Traffic grows to 30,000 QPS.
Upgrade to 64 cores -> ~12,000 QPS, roughly 4x the price.
Next upgrade? There is no 640-core box. And it is still one machine: if it dies, everything dies.
```

Vertical scaling hits a hard ceiling, the cost grows faster than the capacity, and the single machine stays a single point of failure.

### Better design

```text
                 +--> app-1 (3k QPS)
Load balancer ---+--> app-2 (3k QPS)
                 +--> ...
                 +--> app-12 (3k QPS)     -> 36k QPS, and losing one box costs 1/12
```

A load balancer (a component that spreads requests across servers) sends traffic to many identical servers. Capacity grows almost linearly, and one failure only removes a slice.

**Trade-offs:**
- Horizontal scaling needs load balancing, stateless services and, for data, partitioning, which makes consistency harder.
- For databases, scaling up first is often right: modern servers are very large, and one box avoids distributed-data problems.

**Key takeaway:** Scale stateless services out; scale databases up until the numbers force you to partition.

---

## 2. Stateless services

**Definition:** A service is stateless when no per-user data lives in a server's memory or local disk, so any instance can serve any request.

State still exists; it simply moves into stores built for it: sessions into Redis or signed tokens, files into object storage, data into the database.

### The problem

```java
@RestController
class CartController {
    private final Map<String, Cart> carts = new HashMap<>(); // lives in THIS JVM only

    @PostMapping("/cart/{userId}/items")
    void add(@PathVariable String userId, @RequestBody Item item) {
        carts.computeIfAbsent(userId, id -> new Cart()).add(item);
    }
}
```

The user's next request lands on a different server and the cart is empty. A deploy or crash wipes every cart on that box. "Sticky sessions" (always routing a user to the same server) hide the bug but make load uneven and failures painful.

### Better design

```java
@RestController
class CartController {
    private final CartRepository carts;   // backed by Redis or the database

    @PostMapping("/cart/{userId}/items")
    void add(@PathVariable String userId, @RequestBody Item item) {
        carts.addItem(userId, item);      // any instance can serve the next request
    }
}
```

Now servers can be added, removed or replaced at any time, which is what autoscaling needs.

**Key takeaway:** Push state out of the app tier so app servers become interchangeable.

---

## 3. Availability and the nines

**Definition:** Availability is the fraction of time the system serves requests successfully, usually written as "nines".

Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by 10x, and usually costs far more than the previous one.

| Availability | Downtime per year | Per 30-day month |
|---|---|---|
| 99% | 3.65 days | 7.2 hours |
| 99.9% | 8.77 hours | 43.2 minutes |
| 99.99% | 52.6 minutes | 4.3 minutes |
| 99.999% | 5.26 minutes | 26 seconds |

### The problem

```text
Request path: LB (99.99%) -> App (99.95%) -> DB (99.95%)   -- all required, in series
Total = 0.9999 x 0.9995 x 0.9995 ~ 99.89%
```

Components in series multiply, so the whole is always less available than its weakest part. Each extra synchronous dependency lowers the total.

### Better design

```text
Two independent replicas, either can serve (in parallel):
  1 - (1 - 0.99)^2 = 1 - 0.0001 = 99.99%
```

Redundancy lifts availability, but only if the failures are independent: different racks, availability zones (separate datacenters in a region) or regions, with no shared dependency.

**Key takeaway:** Series multiplies down, parallel redundancy multiplies up.

### SLI vs. SLO vs. SLA

- **SLI (indicator):** what you measure, e.g. the share of requests that succeed in under 300 ms.
- **SLO (objective):** the internal target, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days. The error budget is 1 - SLO.
- **SLA (agreement):** the external promise with penalties, usually looser than the SLO.

---

## 4. Single points of failure and redundancy

**Definition:** A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure stops the whole system.

Redundancy means running spare copies so a failure is absorbed. Common forms are N+1 instances (one more than needed), database replicas with automatic failover, and redundant load balancers.

### The problem

```text
Users -> LB -> [app x 6] -> one DB primary (no replica)
                          -> one Redis node
```

Six app servers look redundant, but the database and the cache are each one box. Lose either and the six app servers have nothing to talk to.

### Better design

```text
Users -> LB pair -> [app x 6 across 3 AZs] -> DB primary (AZ-a) + standby (AZ-b), auto failover
                                            -> Redis primary + replica, auto failover
Health checks remove dead instances; autoscaling replaces them.
```

**Trade-offs:**
- More copies cost money, and failover is not instant (often seconds to a minute for a database).

**Key takeaway:** Walk every box on the diagram and ask "what if this one dies?".

---

## 5. Reliability vs. availability

**Definition:** Reliability is the system doing the right thing over time, including never losing or corrupting data; availability is just being up.

A cash machine that is always on but sometimes dispenses the wrong amount is available but not reliable.

### The problem

```text
Payment service: 99.99% available.
A retry after a timeout charges the customer twice. A cache bug serves another user's order.
```

Every request got a fast response, so availability looks perfect, yet the system is wrong.

### Better design

```text
- Idempotency keys so retries cannot double-charge
- Replicated, durable writes (acknowledge only after the data is safely stored)
- Staged rollouts and fast rollback for software bugs
- Availability ~ MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)
```

MTBF is the mean time between failures; MTTR is the mean time to recovery. Cutting MTTR (fast detection, one-click rollback) is often cheaper than making failures rarer.

### Fault vs. failure

- **Fault:** one component misbehaves (a disk dies, a node hangs).
- **Failure:** the whole system stops serving users.
- **Fault tolerance** is the art of keeping faults from becoming failures.

**Key takeaway:** Up is not the same as correct; design for both.

---

## 6. Latency percentiles

**Definition:** Latency is the time to serve one request; percentiles describe its distribution, such as p99 = 99% of requests are faster than this.

Averages hide the slow tail. Track p50 (the median), p95, p99 and sometimes p99.9.

### The problem

```text
Average latency 40 ms, looks great. But p99 = 2 s.
A page calls 100 backends in parallel; each is slow 1% of the time.
Chance at least one is slow = 1 - 0.99^100 ~ 63% of page loads
```

Fan-out (one request calling many services) turns a rare slow call into a common slow page. Heavy users, often your best customers, hit the tail most.

### Better design

```text
- Set an SLO on p99, not the average
- Timeouts and deadlines on every call
- Hedged requests: if no reply by the p95 time, send a copy to another replica; use the first answer
- Cache, colocate data near users, precompute, and reduce sequential round trips
```

**Key takeaway:** Measure and promise percentiles, never averages.

---

## 7. Throughput and utilisation

**Definition:** Throughput is how many requests per second the system completes; it is different from latency, which is how long each one takes.

A highway's throughput is cars per hour; latency is your travel time. Pushing more cars on raises throughput only until jams form, and then travel time explodes.

### The problem

```text
Server at 95% CPU utilisation. A small burst arrives.
Requests queue; queueing delay grows sharply as utilisation nears 100%.
p99 jumps from 50 ms to 3 s even though throughput barely rose.
```

Little's law (L = arrival rate x time in system) ties them together: when requests stay longer, more of them pile up in the system.

### Better design

Run critical resources at about 50-70% utilisation, autoscale on that signal, and shed load (reject early with 429 or 503) rather than queueing forever.

**Trade-offs:**
- Batching raises throughput but adds latency; spare headroom costs money.

**Key takeaway:** Keep headroom; latency explodes near 100% utilisation.

---

## 8. Graceful degradation

**Definition:** When a part fails, keep the core working with reduced features instead of failing completely.

A restaurant out of one dish still serves the rest of the menu.

### The problem

```text
Product page = product info + price + reviews + recommendations
Recommendations service times out after 30 s -> the whole page returns 500.
```

A non-critical feature took down the critical path.

### Better design

```text
Recommendations: 200 ms timeout + circuit breaker -> fall back to "top sellers" (cached)
Reviews:         serve stale cached reviews, or hide the section
Product + price: critical; served from DB/cache with replicas
```

A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a while so it can recover. The page still sells the product.

**Key takeaway:** Decide in advance what is critical and what can be dropped.

---

## In an HLD interview

- **URL Shortener / API Gateway:** stateless app tier behind a load balancer; redirects stay available even when analytics is down.
- **Payment System:** reliability beats availability; idempotency keys and durable writes before saying "success".
- **News Feed / Amazon E-commerce:** graceful degradation; the feed or product page works without recommendations or ads.
- **Google Search / Metrics:** fan-out to many shards makes p99 the real target; use timeouts and hedged requests.
- **What to SAY:** "The app tier is stateless so it scales out; I'll remove each SPOF with replicas across zones, target p99 latency, and degrade non-critical features first."

## At a glance

| Concept | Core idea | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Vertical vs horizontal | Bigger box vs more boxes | Have I hit the single-box ceiling? |
| Stateless services | State lives in stores, not servers | Can any instance serve this request? |
| Availability | Series multiplies down, parallel up | How many nines, and through which path? |
| SPOF / redundancy | Spare copies in separate zones | What if this box dies? |
| Reliability | Correct over time, no data loss | Can a retry or bug corrupt data? |
| Latency percentiles | p99, not average | What does the slowest 1% see? |
| Throughput | Requests completed per second | Am I running too close to 100%? |
| Graceful degradation | Drop extras, keep the core | What can fail without hurting the main flow? |

## Final memory aid

- **Scale out** stateless apps; **scale up** databases first
- **State** goes to Redis, the DB or object storage
- **Series** multiplies down; **redundancy** multiplies up
- **Every box** can die: find the SPOFs
- **Up** is not the same as **correct**
- **p99**, never the average
- **50-70%** utilisation keeps latency calm
- **Degrade**, do not die

items.title: Networking essentials: DNS, TCP/UDP, HTTP, TLS and proxies
items.summary: Every arrow on a system design diagram is a network hop with its own costs: finding the address, opening a connection, encrypting it, and passing through proxies. Knowing what happens at each step explains where latency comes from, why connection reuse matters, and where to put caching, security and routing. This chapter walks through each layer with a small failure and its fix, then ties them together in "what happens when you type a URL".
items.markdown:
Every arrow on a system design diagram is a network hop with its own costs: finding the address, opening a connection, encrypting it, and passing through proxies. Knowing what happens at each step explains where latency comes from, why connection reuse matters, and where to put caching, security and routing. This chapter walks through each layer with a small failure and its fix, then ties them together in "what happens when you type a URL".

## 1. DNS resolution and TTL

**Definition:** DNS (Domain Name System) turns a name like `api.example.com` into an IP address, and caches the answer for a time called the TTL (time to live).

It works like a phone directory with many local copies. Your browser and OS keep a cache; on a miss, a recursive resolver (usually your ISP's or a public one like 8.8.8.8) asks the root servers, then the `.com` servers, then the domain's authoritative server, and caches the result.

### The problem

```text
api.example.com  A  203.0.113.10   TTL 86400   (24 hours)
The server at 203.0.113.10 dies; you switch the record to 203.0.113.20.
Resolvers and clients keep using the old IP for up to a day.
```

A long TTL means failover through DNS is slow. Some clients also cache beyond the TTL, so DNS changes are never instant.

### Better design

```text
api.example.com  A  203.0.113.10   TTL 60      health-checked, auto-switches on failure
Global traffic:  geo/latency-based DNS returns the nearest healthy region
Instant failover: anycast IP or a global load balancer in front, so the IP never changes
```

**Trade-offs:**
- Short TTLs mean more DNS queries and slightly slower first requests; long TTLs mean slow changes.

**Key takeaway:** TTL is a dial between fast failover and fewer lookups.

---

## 2. TCP vs. UDP

**Definition:** TCP is a connection-based protocol that delivers bytes reliably and in order; UDP sends independent packets with no delivery or ordering guarantee.

TCP is registered post with tracking and redelivery; UDP is shouting across a room. TCP starts with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) that costs one round trip before any data flows.

### The problem

```text
Video call over TCP: one packet is lost.
TCP holds back every later packet until the lost one is resent (~1 round trip).
The call freezes, then plays stale audio that is no longer useful.
```

This is head-of-line blocking: one lost packet delays everything behind it. For live media, late data is worse than missing data.

### Better design

```text
Live video/voice, games -> UDP (or WebRTC on top of it): skip lost packets, keep going
DNS lookups             -> UDP (small, single request/response; retry if lost)
APIs, DB connections    -> TCP: correctness and order matter
HTTP/3                  -> QUIC over UDP, with its own reliability per stream
```

**Key takeaway:** Use TCP when every byte matters, UDP when freshness matters more.

---

## 3. HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3

**Definition:** Three versions of the same request/response protocol that differ in how many requests can share one connection and how they handle packet loss.

| Version | Transport | Key idea | Weak spot |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP/1.1 | TCP | One request at a time per connection; keep-alive | Browsers open ~6 connections per host |
| HTTP/2 | TCP | Many streams multiplexed on one connection; binary; header compression | One lost TCP packet stalls all streams |
| HTTP/3 | QUIC (UDP) | Independent streams; transport and TLS handshake combined | Some networks block or throttle UDP |

### The problem

A page needs 80 small files over HTTP/1.1. With ~6 connections, requests wait in line behind each other, and each new connection pays its own handshakes.

### Better design

HTTP/2 sends all 80 requests at once over one connection. HTTP/3 also stops a single lost packet from stalling every stream, and survives a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data (connection migration). gRPC runs on HTTP/2 because it needs multiplexed, bidirectional streams.

**Key takeaway:** HTTP/2 fixes application-level queueing; HTTP/3 also fixes TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

---

## 4. Keep-alive and connection pooling

**Definition:** Keep-alive reuses an open connection for many requests; a connection pool keeps a set of open connections ready for reuse.

Opening a connection is like dialling a call: you pay setup time before you can talk. Reusing it skips that cost.

### The problem

```java
// creates a new client (and new connections) for every call
String getPrice(String sku) throws Exception {
    HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(PRICE_URL + sku)).build();
    return client.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
}
```

Every call pays a TCP handshake plus a TLS handshake. At 5,000 calls/s that wastes CPU on both sides, and can exhaust ephemeral ports.

### Better design

```java
private static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))
        .build();                         // shared; pools and reuses connections

String getPrice(String sku) throws Exception {
    HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(PRICE_URL + sku))
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build();
    return CLIENT.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
}
```

One shared client keeps connections open and adds timeouts. Database connection pools (such as HikariCP) apply the same idea and also cap how many connections hit the database.

**Key takeaway:** Create clients once, reuse connections, and always set timeouts.

---

## 5. TLS handshake

**Definition:** TLS (Transport Layer Security, the "S" in HTTPS) encrypts traffic, detects tampering, and proves the server's identity with a certificate.

During the handshake the client and server agree on keys, and the server presents a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority (CA). TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for this; TLS 1.2 needed two.

### The problem

```text
User in India, server in the US, round trip ~200 ms. Cold HTTPS request:
  TCP handshake          1 RTT   200 ms
  TLS 1.2 handshake      2 RTT   400 ms
  HTTP request/response  1 RTT   200 ms
                                 ~800 ms before the first byte of the page
```

### Better design

```text
TLS 1.3                        -> 1 RTT for the handshake (0-RTT on resumption, replay-safe requests only)
Terminate TLS at a nearby edge -> the handshakes cross ~20 ms, not 200 ms
Reuse connections              -> handshake paid once, not per request
Inside the network             -> re-encrypt or use mTLS (both sides present certificates)
```

TLS termination means decrypting at the load balancer or CDN. mTLS (mutual TLS) is the standard way services prove identity to each other in a service mesh.

**Key takeaway:** Handshakes cost round trips; terminate near the user and reuse connections.

---

## 6. Forward vs. reverse proxy

**Definition:** A forward proxy acts for clients going out; a reverse proxy acts for servers, receiving traffic coming in.

A forward proxy is a company's reception desk that places outside calls for employees. A reverse proxy is a hotel front desk that receives every visitor and sends them to the right room.

### The problem

```text
Internet -> app-1 (public IP)
Internet -> app-2 (public IP)
Internet -> app-3 (public IP)
```

Every server is exposed, each handles its own TLS certificate, clients must know which one to call, and there is no single place for rate limiting or routing.

### Better design

```nginx
upstream app { server 10.0.1.11:8080; server 10.0.1.12:8080; server 10.0.1.13:8080; }

server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;                 # TLS terminated here
    location /api/ { proxy_pass http://app; }       # load balanced
    location /static/ { root /var/www; expires 7d; } # served and cached here
}
```

The reverse proxy (Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy, a cloud load balancer or an API gateway) handles TLS, load balancing, routing, caching, rate limiting and logging, and hides the internal servers.

### Forward proxy vs. reverse proxy

- **Forward:** sits next to clients; the server sees the proxy's IP. Used for egress filtering and outbound caching.
- **Reverse:** sits next to servers; the client sees only the proxy. Used for load balancing, TLS and routing.
- **Sidecar:** in a service mesh each service gets its own local proxy for service-to-service traffic.

**Key takeaway:** Put a reverse proxy in front of every fleet of servers.

---

## 7. NAT

**Definition:** NAT (Network Address Translation) lets many devices with private IP addresses share one public IP address.

Private ranges such as `10.0.0.0/8` and `192.168.0.0/16` are not routable on the internet. The NAT device rewrites outgoing packets to its public IP and remembers a port mapping so replies find their way back, like a company switchboard with one external number.

### The problem

```text
Phone (192.168.1.5) behind home router NAT.
Chat server tries to open a connection TO the phone to deliver a message.
There is no mapping for unsolicited inbound traffic -> dropped.
```

Servers cannot start connections to clients behind NAT. Idle mappings also expire, silently breaking long-lived connections.

### Better design

```text
Client opens the connection outward (WebSocket / long-lived TCP) and keeps it alive
with periodic heartbeats (e.g. every 30-60 s); the server pushes messages down it.
Cloud: app servers in private subnets reach the internet through a NAT gateway
       but cannot be reached directly from it.
```

Peer-to-peer calls use helper techniques (STUN to discover the public address, TURN to relay when direct paths fail).

**Key takeaway:** Behind NAT, the client must dial out; the server cannot dial in.

---

## 8. What happens when you type a URL

**Definition:** The full journey of `https://shop.example.com/cart` from keypress to rendered page.

### The sequence

```text
1. DNS:   browser cache -> OS cache -> recursive resolver -> root -> .com -> authoritative
          -> IP of the nearest CDN edge (via geo-DNS or anycast)
2. TCP:   SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK                                  (1 RTT)
3. TLS:   TLS 1.3 handshake, certificate checked             (1 RTT; QUIC merges 2+3)
4. HTTP:  GET /cart sent over the encrypted connection
5. Edge:  CDN serves cached static parts; forwards /cart to the origin
6. Origin: load balancer / reverse proxy -> stateless app server -> cache / DB
7. Back:  response flows back; browser parses HTML, fetches CSS/JS/images
          over the SAME connection (HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplexing)
8. Render: page painted; the connection stays open for the next click
```

### Common mistake

Listing only "DNS, then the server responds". Interviewers want the round trips counted and the places where each cost is cut: DNS caching, edge TLS termination, connection reuse and caching at every layer.

**Key takeaway:** Count the round trips, then show where each one is saved.

---

## In an HLD interview

- **Netflix / YouTube:** geo-DNS or anycast to the nearest CDN edge, TLS terminated at the edge, HTTP/3 for lossy mobile networks.
- **Chat / WhatsApp / Ride Tracking:** clients behind NAT keep a long-lived WebSocket open with heartbeats; servers push over it.
- **API Gateway / Rate Limiter:** a reverse proxy layer handles TLS, routing, auth and rate limiting before traffic reaches services.
- **Payment System / microservices:** pooled connections with timeouts between services, and mTLS inside the network.
- **What to SAY:** "Users resolve to the nearest edge via DNS; TLS terminates there; behind it a reverse proxy load-balances to stateless services over pooled, mTLS connections."

## At a glance

| Concept | Core idea | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| DNS and TTL | Name to IP, cached for TTL | How fast must failover be? |
| TCP vs UDP | Reliable order vs fresh speed | Is late data worse than lost data? |
| HTTP/1.1, 2, 3 | Multiplexing, then per-stream recovery | Are requests queueing behind each other? |
| Keep-alive / pooling | Reuse connections | Am I paying handshakes on every call? |
| TLS handshake | Encrypt, verify, costs round trips | Where do I terminate TLS? |
| Forward vs reverse proxy | Acts for clients vs for servers | Which side does this proxy protect? |
| NAT | Many private IPs share one public IP | Who opens the connection? |
| Typing a URL | DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, edge, origin | How many round trips, and which can I save? |

## Final memory aid

- **DNS:** name to IP; TTL trades failover speed for lookups
- **TCP:** reliable and ordered; **UDP:** fast and fresh
- **HTTP/2** multiplexes; **HTTP/3** avoids TCP head-of-line blocking
- **Reuse** connections; always set timeouts
- **TLS 1.3:** one round trip; terminate near the user
- **Reverse proxy** guards servers; **forward proxy** guards clients
- **NAT:** clients dial out, servers push back

items.title: Load balancing
items.summary: A load balancer sits in front of a group of servers and spreads incoming requests across them, so no single server is overwhelmed and a dead server stops receiving traffic. It is what makes "just add more servers" actually work. This chapter covers the two kinds of load balancer, the common algorithms, health checks, why sticky sessions cause trouble, global load balancing, and how to stop the load balancer itself from becoming the weak point.
items.markdown:
A load balancer sits in front of a group of servers and spreads incoming requests across them, so no single server is overwhelmed and a dead server stops receiving traffic. It is what makes "just add more servers" actually work. This chapter covers the two kinds of load balancer, the common algorithms, health checks, why sticky sessions cause trouble, global load balancing, and how to stop the load balancer itself from becoming the weak point.

## 1. What a load balancer does

**Definition:** A load balancer (LB) is a component that receives client traffic and forwards each connection or request to one of several healthy backend servers.

Think of the host at a busy restaurant. Guests do not pick a table and a waiter themselves; the host spreads them across sections and skips the section whose waiter has gone home. Clients only know one address (the LB), so you can add, remove or replace servers behind it without telling anyone.

### The problem

```text
Clients --> app-1 (single server, 2,000 req/s capacity)
Traffic at peak: 5,000 req/s
```

One server cannot take 5,000 requests per second. If you start a second and third server, clients still need to know which one to call, and when app-2 crashes they keep calling it.

### Better design

```text
                 +--> app-1 (healthy)
Clients --> LB --+--> app-2 (failed health check, skipped)
                 +--> app-3 (healthy)
                 +--> app-4 (healthy)
```

Clients call one stable address. The LB spreads 5,000 req/s over the healthy servers and quietly routes around app-2 until it recovers.

**Trade-offs:**
- One more network hop (usually well under a millisecond inside a data center).
- One more component that must itself be highly available (see section 9).

**Key takeaway:** A load balancer gives you one stable entry point, horizontal scaling and automatic failover in a single box on the diagram.

---

## 2. L4 vs. L7 load balancing

**Definition:** An L4 load balancer routes by network information (IP address and port); an L7 load balancer understands the application protocol, usually HTTP, and routes by path, host, headers or cookies.
